title: The RBI Held Rates While the Rupee Hit Historic Lows. Here Is What It Means for Every NRI.
excerpt: Repo rate stays at 5.25 per cent for a third straight meeting. The rupee is at 96.72, oil is near $96, and the central bank is betting the Gulf crisis will cool before inflation forces a hike.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India on Friday held its benchmark repo rate steady at 5.25 per cent, pausing for a third consecutive meeting as policymakers chose to look past the rupee's relentless slide and assess the broader fallout from the Gulf conflict on inflation and growth.

All six members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted unanimously to keep rates unchanged. The panel also maintained its "neutral" stance, signalling that it is neither leaning toward a cut nor committing to a hike — a wait-and-see posture that disappointed some currency traders who had been positioning for a more hawkish turn.

"The global environment has deteriorated," RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said while announcing the decision. "It is prudent to wait until greater clarity emerges."

## The numbers behind the pause

India's benchmark 10-year bond yield edged lower to 6.96 per cent after the announcement. The rupee weakened to 96.72 against the dollar, continuing a decline that has now exceeded 6 per cent since the start of 2026. The Nifty 50 added 0.18 per cent to 23,459 and the Sensex gained 0.2 per cent to 74,515, with rate-sensitive financials and realty stocks leading the modest advance.

The decision came against a backdrop of acute pressure. Brent crude remains elevated near $96 a barrel, driven by the US-Iran conflict that has disrupted shipping near the Strait of Hormuz since late February. Record foreign fund outflows have compounded the rupee's weakness, and several of India's regional peers — Indonesia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka — have already raised rates to defend their own currencies.

The RBI has instead relied on aggressive foreign exchange interventions, selling dollars in the spot market while simultaneously conducting buy-sell swaps to prevent those interventions from draining domestic rupee liquidity. One-year hedging costs have fallen from a mid-May peak of 3.50 per cent to 2.92 per cent, a drop that some traders believe was deliberately engineered ahead of the policy announcement.

## What it means for NRIs

For the diaspora, the RBI's decision creates a mixed picture that depends heavily on which side of the remittance equation you sit on.

**Sending money to India**: The rupee at 96.72 means every dollar converts into more rupees than at any point in history. NRIs remitting money for family support, property purchases, or fixed deposits are getting a historically favourable exchange rate. The RBI's decision not to hike rates means this weakness is likely to persist in the near term, so the window remains open.

**Investing in Indian markets**: The hold signals that the RBI is prioritising growth over currency defence, which is broadly supportive of equity markets. Financials and realty, which rallied 1.2 per cent and 1.4 per cent respectively after the announcement, benefit directly from stable borrowing costs. But the elevated oil bill and foreign outflows remain headwinds. The Nifty has lost 2.6 per cent over the past seven sessions.

**NRI fixed deposits**: With the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent, banks are unlikely to raise deposit rates in the near term. NRI fixed deposit rates, which currently range between 6.5 and 7.5 per cent for one-year terms depending on the bank, will hold steady. The real return, however, is being eroded by the rupee's depreciation — a 7 per cent FD yield loses its edge if the rupee falls another 3-4 per cent by the time the deposit matures.

**FCNR deposits**: Foreign Currency Non-Resident deposits, denominated in dollars or other foreign currencies, avoid the rupee depreciation risk entirely. With the rupee under pressure, FCNR deposits offer a hedge that becomes more attractive the longer the Gulf crisis persists.

## The road ahead

Governor Malhotra noted that while inflation is expected to rise, underlying price pressures remain "benign" for now. But he warned that second-round effects of higher energy prices "warrant vigil." The Wall Street Journal reported that nine of eleven economists surveyed expected the hold, with two forecasting a 25-basis-point hike.

The consensus among analysts is that the RBI is preserving its ammunition. If oil stays above $95 and the rupee breaks past 98, a rate hike becomes increasingly likely at the August meeting. Indonesia's 50-basis-point hike last month — its first in years — serves as a template for what an emergency response could look like.

For NRI investors, the takeaway is straightforward. The RBI is betting that the Gulf crisis will cool before inflation forces its hand. If that bet pays off, Indian equities and the rupee could recover ground in the second half of the year. If it does not, the central bank will have waited too long, and the correction will be sharper for the delay.

*Sources: Reserve Bank of India monetary policy statement, June 5 2026; Reuters; Wall Street Journal; LiveMint*
